text: Functions and modules: #[pyfunction] , #[pymodule] Step 1 of the token counter: the root program's token loop as plain Rust, and a thin function Python can call. ext/src/lib.rs /// Tokens = maximal runs of ASCII letters or digits (rule 3 of PROGRAM.md). /// Non-ASCII characters are UTF-8 bytes >= 0x80, so a byte loop gives the char answer. fn tokens(s: &[u8]) -> u64 { let mut n = 0; let mut inside = false ; for &b in s { let t = b.is_ascii_alphanumeric(); if t && !inside { n += 1; } inside = t; } n } ext/src/lib.rs /// Step 1: one message per call. `&str` borrows the Python string's UTF-8 bytes. #[pyfunction] fn count_tokens(text: &str) -> u64 { tokens(text.as_bytes()) } #[pyfunction] generates the glue: a C-level function that takes Python's argument objects, converts each to the Rust parameter type ( &str here), calls your function, and converts the u64 result back into a Python int .

section: 9. free-threaded python: what an extension must declare and protect
text: The fix is the Rust way of sharing: make the class frozen (no &mut self , so no borrow flag) and put the mutable part behind a Mutex (or atomics), which makes threads wait their turn instead of failing: ext/src/lib.rs /// The thread-safe version: `frozen` means no `&mut self` ever, so PyO3 needs no /// run-time borrow flag; the mutable state sits behind a Mutex that threads queue on. #[pyclass(module = "tokrs" , frozen)] struct SharedCounter { per_user: std::sync::Mutex<HashMap<String, u64>>, } #[pymethods] impl SharedCounter { #[new] fn new() -> Self { SharedCounter { per_user: std::sync::Mutex::new(HashMap::new()) } } fn add(& self , user: &str, text: &str) { let n = tokens(text.as_bytes()); // count outside the lock * self .per_user.lock().unwrap().entry(user.to_owned()).or_insert(0) += n; } #[getter] fn total(& self ) -> u64 { self .per_user.lock().unwrap().values().sum() } } The token counting happens before lock() , so threads only queue for the short dictionary update.
